question: Your vehicle starts to skid. What is the first thing you should do?
options: Release the brake pedal fully or ease off the accelerator
Steer sharply against the direction of the skid
explanation: Skids are caused by the driver braking, accelerating or steering too harshly or driving too fast for the road conditions. If skidding occurs, remove the cause by releasing the brake pedal fully or easing off the accelerator. Turn the steering wheel in the direction of the skid. (Highway Code rule 119.)

question: Your car has anti-lock brakes (ABS). In an emergency stop you should…
options: Brake gently to avoid triggering the system
Apply the handbrake at the same time
Apply the footbrake firmly and keep it applied until you have slowed sufficiently
explanation: ABS. If your vehicle is fitted with anti-lock brakes, you should follow the advice in the vehicle handbook. However, in the case of an emergency, apply the footbrake firmly; do not release the pressure until the vehicle has slowed to the desired speed. (Highway Code rule 120.)

question: After driving through deep water, what should you do?
options: Switch the engine off and on again
Drive faster to dry the brakes
Apply the handbrake firmly several times
Test your brakes gently at the first safe opportunity
explanation: Brakes affected by water. If you have driven through deep water your brakes may be less effective. Test them at the first safe opportunity by pushing gently on the brake pedal to make sure that they work. (Highway Code rule 121.)

question: Why is coasting (travelling in neutral or with the clutch down) discouraged?
options: It is illegal on all public roads
It causes the brakes to overheat immediately
It removes engine braking and reduces your control of the vehicle
explanation: Coasting. This term describes a vehicle travelling in neutral or with the clutch pressed down. It can reduce driver control because engine braking is eliminated, vehicle speed downhill will increase quickly, increased use of the footbrake can reduce its effectiveness, and steering response will be affected. (Highway Code rule 122.)

question: On a dry road carrying fast-moving traffic, what is the minimum time gap you should leave to the vehicle in front?
options: One car length for every 10 mph
explanation: Stopping distances. Drive at a speed that will allow you to stop well within the distance you can see to be clear. Leave enough space between you and the vehicle in front so that you can pull up safely if it suddenly slows down or stops — the safe rule is never to get closer than the overall stopping distance. Allow at least a two-second gap on roads carrying fast-moving traffic; the gap should be at least doubled on wet roads and increased still further on icy roads (up to ten times). (Highway Code rule 126.)

question: You MUST use headlights when visibility is seriously reduced. The Highway Code defines this as generally being unable to see for more than…
explanation: You MUST use headlights when visibility is seriously reduced — generally when you cannot see for more than 100 metres (328 feet). You may also use front or rear fog lights but you MUST switch them off when visibility improves. (Highway Code rule 226.)

question: In wet weather, your steering suddenly feels light and unresponsive. What is the most likely cause and what should you do?
options: Aquaplaning — ease off the accelerator and slow down gradually
Power steering failure — pull over and call for recovery
explanation: Wet weather. In wet weather, stopping distances will be at least double those required for stopping on dry roads. You should keep well back from the vehicle in front, ease off the accelerator and slow down gradually if the steering becomes unresponsive (aquaplaning), and be aware that the rain and spray from vehicles may make it difficult to see and be seen. (Highway Code rule 227.)

question: On icy or snowy roads, by how much can stopping distances increase compared with dry roads?
explanation: When driving in icy or snowy weather, drive with care, even if the roads have been treated; keep well back from the road user in front as stopping distances can be ten times greater than on dry roads; take care when overtaking vehicles spreading salt; watch out for snowploughs which may throw out snow on either side. (Highway Code rule 230.)

question: When driving on ice, the Highway Code advises you to drive at a slow speed in…
options: As high a gear as possible
As low a gear as possible
explanation: Drive extremely carefully when the roads are icy. Avoid sudden actions as these could cause loss of control. You should drive at a slow speed in as high a gear as possible; accelerate and brake very gently; drive particularly slowly on bends; check your grip on the road surface when there is snow or ice by choosing a safe place to brake gently. (Highway Code rule 231.)

question: Why MUST you switch off rear fog lights when visibility improves?
options: They are linked to the speed limiter
They can dazzle following drivers and obscure your brake lights
They cause your headlights to dim
explanation: You MUST NOT use front or rear fog lights unless visibility is seriously reduced, as they dazzle other road users and can obscure your brake lights. You MUST switch them off when visibility improves. (Highway Code rule 236.)

question: In a contraflow system at road works, what should you do?
options: Use the closed lane to overtake
Reduce your speed and increase the distance to the vehicle in front
explanation: Contraflow systems mean that you may be travelling in a narrower lane than normal and with no permanent barrier between you and oncoming traffic. Reduce your speed and increase the distance to the vehicle in front. (Highway Code rule 290.)
